---
title: "Co-evolution of networks and behaviour"
author: "Tom A.B. Snijders and Christian Steglich"
description: >
  Behaviour as a dependent variable: separate selection from influence,
  check the fit of the model, and interpret influence with influence tables.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# RSiena writes report files to the working directory; keep them out of the site.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = tempdir())
```

Do adolescents choose friends who drink like them (*selection*),
or do they start to drink like their friends (*influence*)?
Both processes make friends similar,
so a cross-sectional analysis cannot separate them.
A SAOM with the network and the behaviour as dependent variables
can (Steglich, Snijders and Pearson, 2010).

This article is based on the scripts `Rscript04SienaBehaviour.R`
by Tom Snijders and `Lab_coevolution.R`
by Christian Steglich and Tom Snijders.

> Steglich, C.E.G., Snijders, T.A.B. and Pearson, M. (2010).
> Dynamic networks and behavior: Separating selection from influence.
> *Sociological Methodology*, 40, 329–393.
> <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2010.01225.x>

## Data

The `s50` data have friendship at three waves,
and smoking and alcohol use at the same three waves.
Here, friendship, smoking and drinking are all dependent variables.

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(RSiena)
friendship <- as_dependent_rsiena(array(c(s501, s502, s503),
                                        dim = c(50, 50, 3)))
drinking <- as_dependent_rsiena(s50a, type = "behavior")
smoking  <- as_dependent_rsiena(s50s, type = "behavior")
mydata <- make_data_rsiena(friendship, smoking, drinking)
mydata
```

`write_report(mydata)` writes descriptive statistics to a file.
For behaviour variables, it also gives the number of increases
and decreases between waves.
Moran's I and related measures (for example, `nacf()` in the sna package)
describe how similar friends are.

## Specification

The model has three parts, one for each dependent variable.
First the structural effects for friendship:

```{r structural}
myeff <- make_specification(mydata)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(outAct, inPop, transTrip, transRecTrip),
                    verbose = FALSE)
```

Then the **selection** effects:
how smoking and drinking affect the choice of friends.

```{r selection}
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, simX, covar1 = "smoking", verbose = FALSE)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(egoX, altX, egoXaltX, egoSqX),
                    covar1 = "drinking", verbose = FALSE)
```

Then the **influence** effects:
how friends affect smoking and drinking.
These effects belong to the behaviour variables,
so `depvar` must name the behaviour variable.

```{r influence}
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, avAlt, depvar = "drinking",
                    covar1 = "friendship", verbose = FALSE)
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, avSim, depvar = "smoking",
                    covar1 = "friendship", verbose = FALSE)
myeff
```

The effects `egoXaltX` (selection) and `avAlt` (influence) for drinking
are a matching pair, as are `simX` and `avSim` for smoking.
Use such pairs, so that selection and influence are measured
in the same terms.

## Estimation

```{r estimate}
algo <- set_algorithm_saom(seed = 1410)
ans <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = algo, batch = TRUE)
ans
```

Continue the estimation for better convergence and precise standard errors
(see Section 7.3.3 of the manual):

```{r estimate2}
algo2 <- set_algorithm_saom(seed = 828, n3 = 5000, nsub = 1,
                            n2start = 2000, firstg = 0.01)
ans2 <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = algo2,
              prevAns = ans, batch = TRUE)
ans2
```

The influence effect for drinking (`drinking average alter`)
and the selection effect (`drinking ego x drinking alter`)
are estimated together, each controlled for the other.

## Interpreting influence

As for selection, the parameters of a behaviour variable
are easier to read in a table or a plot.
The *influence table* gives the evaluation function of the behaviour
for each value of ego's behaviour (horizontal axis)
and each average value of the friends' behaviour (one curve each):

```{r inftable, message = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
library(autograph)
(influence.drinking <- interpret_influence(ans2, mydata,
                                           "friendship", "drinking"))
plot(influence.drinking)
```

In a ministep, a pupil is more likely to change the behaviour
towards a higher value of this function.
When the friends' average is low, the curves show pressure downwards;
when it is high, pressure upwards.

For smoking, the influence effect is average similarity.
Each curve shows the hypothetical case that *all* friends
have the same value, so real cases are less extreme:

```{r inftable2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(interpret_influence(ans2, mydata, "friendship", "smoking"))
```

Section 14.4 of the manual explains influence tables.

## Goodness of fit

Does the model reproduce features of the data that it does not
model directly?
Simulate from the fitted model with `returnDeps = TRUE`.
No further estimation is needed, so set `nsub = 0`:

```{r gofsim}
algo3 <- set_algorithm_saom(seed = 766, nsub = 0)
ans.gof <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = algo3,
                 prevAns = ans2, returnDeps = TRUE, batch = TRUE)
```

First, is there time heterogeneity?

```{r timetest}
test_time(ans.gof)
```

Then compare statistics of the observed data with the same statistics
of the simulated data.
A small p-value shows a poor fit.

```{r gof, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
gof.out <- test_gof(ans.gof, OutdegreeDistribution, varName = "friendship",
                    cumulative = FALSE, levls = 0:10)
gof.out
plot(gof.out)

gof.in <- test_gof(ans.gof, IndegreeDistribution, varName = "friendship",
                   cumulative = FALSE, levls = 0:10)
gof.in
plot(gof.in)

gof.drink <- test_gof(ans.gof, BehaviorDistribution, varName = "drinking",
                      cumulative = FALSE, levls = 1:5)
gof.drink
plot(gof.drink)
```

`?test_gof_auxiliary` describes more statistics,
for example the triad census and `egoAlterCombi`
for the combination of network and behaviour.

## Alternative influence effects

Average similarity (`avSim`) and total similarity (`totSim`)
are different forms of influence.
With average similarity, the influence of each friend is smaller
when a pupil has more friends;
with total similarity, each friend has the same influence.
To compare, replace one with the other and estimate again:

```{r totsim, eval = FALSE}
myeff.tot <- set_effect(myeff, avSim, depvar = "smoking",
                        covar1 = "friendship", include = FALSE)
myeff.tot <- set_effect(myeff.tot, totSim, depvar = "smoking",
                        covar1 = "friendship")
ans.tot <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff.tot, control_algo = algo,
                 batch = TRUE)
```
